newsitem.title: KENYA: Business angry in Kenya over telecoms crashes.
newsitem.headline: Business angry in Kenya over telecoms crashes.

text.p: Kenya's telecommunications crashed for the second day running on Wednesday, disrupting business and highlighting the inefficiency of state-owned utilities.
The main satellite earth station at Longonot was out of commission for two hours after a 13-hour breakdown on Tuesday.

"Today like yesterday our terminal was not able to access the satellite. We don't know why," Gabriel Gitau, the manager of state-owned Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (KPTC) at Longonot, told Reuters.
Kenya is seeking to attract foreign investment but the decrepit state of its infrastructure -- from roads to water supply -- is a growing impediment.
"This (breakdown) is becoming quite common and seriously affects our operations," the head of foreign exchange dealing at a leading commercial bank in Nairobi said.
"Things are really bad. Communications by telephone is crazy. You can't make good shilling prices because you can't see what competitors are quoting," another bank dealer said.
"I think they are blowing this thing out of proportion," KPTC's public relations manager, Dick Rayori, told Reuters.
"You can only compare our telecoms network with South Africa and some countries in North Africa. We are far ahead of the others in the continent," he said.
Rayori blamed the latest breakdown on a problem at one of Longonot's reference earth stations in the United States.
The East African country's central bank and finance ministry, the engines driving economic reforms, are sharply aware of the negative effect of inefficient public utilities.

"KP&TC would be naive not to know the impact of these problems on financial markets. They have been made fully aware of the position by the central bank and we hope they can work to improve the situation," a finance ministry official said.

Customer complaints against KPTC, aired on a daily basis in letters to newspapers, include the high cost of foreign calls, delays in installing and repairing lines and slow introduction of mobile telephones.
Gitau said about 50 percent of Kenya's telecommunications with the outside world were severed on Tuesday.

"The outage corresponded with a power interruption and the terminal went down. When the power returned it did not come back automatically as it is supposed to," he said, adding that the batteries for back-up supply were "not good".
President Daniel arap Moi said at the start of a British trade fair on Tuesday infrastructure rehabilitation posed "a great challenge" and was one of Kenya's major priorities.
"Infrastructure is known to be deficient in Kenya and corruption is also of concern," Martin Laing, chairman of the British Overseas Trade Board (BOTK), said at the opening.
Ironically, Tuesday's breakdown prevented many businessmen attending the fair from communicating with their home offices.
KPTC is to be split into three entities under a government bill to be presented to parliament in the next weeks.
Rayori said the government was offering 30 percent of the new telcommunications service to foreign and local investors, retaining 70 percent.
"What we are aiming at is to attract private funds to telecoms. For the past seven years we have had a funding crisis," he said.

Kenya's electricity utility, Kenya Power and Lighting Company Limited (KPLC), is unable to meet demand and rations power. Some areas of Nairobi have no electricity for eight hours a day, leading to a surge in generator sales.
About half the capital's 2.5 million residents were without mains water for up to 10 days in March after a pipe burst.
